input.question: Does there exist an absolute constant k such that for every positive integer q one can choose an integer a coprime to q whose continued fraction expansion a/q = [b_0; b_1, ..., b_s] has all partial quotients bounded by k? The paper also records Zaremba's stronger original guess that k = 5.

original_question: Does there exist an absolute constant k such that for every positive integer q one can choose an integer a coprime to q whose continued fraction expansion a/q = [b_0; b_1, ..., b_s] has all partial quotients bounded by k? The paper also records Zaremba's stronger original guess that k = 5.

original_paper.title: On some open problems in Diophantine approximation

rewritten_question: Does there exist an absolute constant k such that for every positive integer q there is an integer a with 1 ≤ a < q and gcd(a, q) = 1 whose finite simple continued fraction expansion a/q = [0; b1, b2, ..., bs] has every partial quotient bounded by k, meaning bj ≤ k for all 1 ≤ j ≤ s? In Zaremba’s stronger original form of the question, can one always take k = 5?

resolution.status_reason: The primary paper presents this as Zaremba’s conjecture and explicitly says it is still open; a later 2023 paper also states that the conjecture remains open, and the bounded later-literature check did not uncover an explicit full resolution of the absolute-constant-for-all-denominators statement.

query_variants: absolute constant bounded partial quotients every denominator
search_trace.notes: Checked the primary source, reviewed later arXiv search results for Zaremba conjecture, and read a 2023 paper whose abstract and introduction explicitly say the conjecture remains open. No bounded-search hit advertised a proof of the full statement for every denominator with one absolute constant.

paper_evidence.quote: The famous Zaremba’s conjecture [154] supposes that there exists an absolute constant k with the following property: for any positive integer q there exists a coprime to q such that in the continued fraction expansion (53) all partial quotients are bounded: bj(a) 6 k, 1 6 j 6 s = s(a). In fact Zaremba conjectured that k = 5.
However Zaremba’s conjecture is still open, and we do not know if for a given q one can get (61) instead of (62), for some a.
Even though Zaremba’s conjecture remains open, Bourgain and Kontorovich solved the problem for a full density subset.
To this day, the conjecture remains unproven.

consulted_papers.title: On some open problems in Diophantine approximation
Zaremba’s Conjecture for Geometric Sequences: An Algorithm
